div.head: EDUCATION ACT AND BOARDS
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT AND BOARDS

OF GUARDIANS. Tux Mayor of Warrington has declared the Education Act of last year impracticable in its working, an opinion which few who are fully acquainted with the terms of the act will endorse. Judging from the opinions expressed at the meetings of the Town Council and the Board of Guardians—the latter of whom appeared to be primarily responsible for the unsatisfactory working of the act—it would seem that the chief difficulty which has arisen is in reference to the payment of school fees by the Guardians for the children of persona not paupers, who are unable through poverty to do so. his Warrington Board of Guardians in this matter of paying school feee, seem to have misconceived the tenor and spirit of the Edueation Act. This board like some others in this and neighbouring conntiee, has in direct violation of the spirit of the act, appointed their relieving officers as inquiry officers, their duty being—with the instruc- tions of the board—to pay the school fees of the children of indigent persons, who are not in receipt of relief from the Union. This mischievous system of appointing relieving officers as inquiry officers, has the effect of bringing into contact the relieving officers and the very poor people who are striving to keep off the books of the parish, and has 'pauperising effect. The appoint- ment of relieving officers to these poste is eondemned by the Local Government Board and their inspectors, who are fully aware of its pernicious effects, For some inconceivable reason the poor persons seek- : inir to obtain the 'school fees for their children have had to attend before the ; Guardians in support of their application. Thle is clearly • gratuitous indignity to those people, who are not to be considered to be in receipt of relief, and who in fact labour under no such disability as do the recipients of parochial relief. This fact the Local Govern- ment Board's Inspector, have impressed on Boards of Guardians generally. To remedy this unhappy blunder, it is only necessary for the Guardians to appoint persons as inquiry officers who are not relieving officers. The duties of inquiry officers are laid down in the appendix to the act, to be, amongst others, "¶OO receive all applications for payment of school fees made to him by parents, not being paupers, resid- ing within the distriet for which he is appointed to act, and forthwith to examine into the circumstances of every ease by visit- ing the house of the applicant, and by lank- tag all net:emery inquiries as regards the means of the applicant. .. To enter the particulars of each come in a book to be termed the school fee application and report book, , . . and to lay euoh book before the Guardian, at their ordinary meet- ings or at any other meetings which he may be requested to attend." Following this comes a description of the duties of the Guardians. The appendix goes on to state, "that the Guardians, on receiving such appli- cations, directly -or through the inquiry ream, give the necessary directions thereon, and where any application is granted, shall also give directions as to the amount of the school fee to be paid, and the time for which the payment is to be made." This shows that although it is necessary that personal appli- cation be made to the Board of Guardians, through the inquiry officer, the whole of the negotiations may be made with that officer, and not be mixed up with the administration of relief, a course repug- nant to the recipients of the fees, as it is at variance with the spirit of the Elementary Education Act, and the wishes of the Local Government Board. The Board of Guardians seem to have been carrying out the terme of the act in the least agreeable manner, and have been oblivious of the fact that the difficulties under which they and the school attendance committee laboured were of their own making. In reply to Mr. Joseph Harrison, a member of the Warrington Board of Guardians, Mr. Fogg. who holds the appointment of relieving officer and inquiry officer, said he had heard no complaints respecting his acting as inquiry officer. Mr. Garrison : 'Do the , people complain to you ?" Mr. Fogg : " Car- -1 iainly not ; but I generally tind they want ; something else besides the school fees when ' they come to me." This last admission shows how incompatible is the performance of the duties of the relieving officer with those of an inquiry officer, and that poor people who are led to believe they are in receipt of relief if they get threepence a week for school fees, will be ready applicants for relief of, mush more substantial character. It is to I be hoped that we have demonstrated that the payment of school fees and the distribu- I don of other kinds of relief are of a t. tally different character ; that personal appli- cation to Guardians of the poor is un- necessary; and that the dual appointment of inquiry officer and relieving officer, intro- duces the latter to a elate of persons who are ever ready to avail themselves of the poor rates, and with whom a relieving officer cennot have WO little intercourse.
